title: A security researcher has traced about 16,500 scans of a UN statistics site to what they call highly likely OpenAI agents.  Rowan H-J posted
text:
A security researcher has traced about 16,500 scans of a UN statistics site to what they call highly likely OpenAI agents.

Rowan H-J posted the work on 26 September. The target was UNCTADstat, the data site of the UN Conference on Trade and Development. The scans ran through a public URL scanner called Urlquery.

The main link to OpenAI comes from the logs of two small public wikis. 54 Azure addresses made UNCTAD-related edits and searches there. 45 of them also edited DseWiki during the wiki swarm, which OpenAI has confirmed was its agents. Some payload pages carried names like CHATGPTTEST1.

The agents appear to have been able to send only GET requests. So they wrote small web pages that made the requests for them, and later used Google's XSS training game as the host. One endpoint only accepts POST. They got around that by double-encoding one letter of its name, and used the trick 55 times. They also split words like POST into pieces to dodge a filter that did not exist.

The author says the agents acted like someone, or something, that won't take no for an answer. They told UNCTAD's security team about the encoding bypass before publishing.

What stands out is the pace. 16,500 scans over the 68 days from 13 April to 19 June is about 240 a day. The author also found 82 rate-limited requests, and the scans kept coming.

title: Cloudflare just released its answer to Jev - and its smaller model can make a decision in ~39 milliseconds.  A few weeks ago, TypeSafe intro
text:
Cloudflare just released its answer to Jev - and its smaller model can make a decision in ~39 milliseconds.

A few weeks ago, TypeSafe introduced Jev and made an interesting argument: most AI workloads don't actually need an LLM to generate paragraphs of text.

Sometimes you just need the model to make a decision.

Cloudflare apparently liked the idea enough to build its own version.

They're called Clef and Clef-Flash, and instead of generating an answer token-by-token, they receive a state + a predefined set of possible decisions and return probabilities for every option in a single pass. Cloudflare Blog

Think:

support ticket → urgent: 94%

security incident → critical: 71%

customer request → billing team: 87%

No reasoning essay.
No JSON generation.
No output parsing.
Just a decision your software can immediately act on.
And the performance numbers are pretty interesting.

Cloudflare benchmarked Clef against Jev on TypeSafe's own workflow evaluations.

The larger Clef beat Jev on 3 of the 4 tested workflow areas: invoice processing, customer service and security incidents. Jev remained ahead on agent-trace observability. Cloudflare Blog

But latency might be the bigger story.

Across Cloudflare's 43-eval run:

Jev - 524ms median

Clef - 209ms

Clef-Flash - 38.8ms

So Clef-Flash was roughly 13× faster than Jev by median request latency in Cloudflare's tests. Cloudflare Blog

The architecture is also surprisingly straightforward.

Clef starts from Qwen3.8-27B, while Clef-Flash uses Qwen3.5-9B.

Cloudflare freezes most of the underlying Qwen model and trains adapters plus a specialized decision head that scores all valid choices directly from the model's internal representations.

The decision itself is non-autoregressive.

That's where a lot of the speed comes from: there's simply no paragraph waiting to be generated before your application gets its answer. Cloudflare Blog

Both models are multimodal too.

They can make decisions from text, JSON, images or video, which makes this much more interesting for agents than another glorified text classifier. Hugging Face

And Cloudflare made another smart move:

the API is compatible with Jev/SystemOne.

So applications already experimenting with Jev can swap Clef in without redesigning the entire decision layer. Hugging Face

Both models are also completely open-source under Apache 2.0 and can be run locally instead of going through Cloudflare.

This whole category is becoming interesting very quickly.

Frontier LLMs are great when an agent needs to reason, code or create something new.

But an agent might make hundreds of tiny decisions for every genuinely difficult problem it encounters.

Which tool should I call?
Where should this ticket go?
Is this transaction suspicious?
Should this workflow continue?
Which of these 50 actions fits the current state?

Using a giant autoregressive LLM for every one of those decisions starts looking increasingly wasteful.

Maybe the future agent stack isn't one enormous model doing everything.
It's a slow reasoning model at the top — and extremely fast decision models handling everything underneath it.

I dropped both models + the technical details in Telegram ↓

title: Anthropic just turned 950 autonomous Claude agents loose on 1.9 billion protein clusters for 21.5 hours. The result wasn't a hallucinated mo
text:
Anthropic just turned 950 autonomous Claude agents loose on 1.9 billion protein clusters for 21.5 hours. The result wasn't a hallucinated molecule or a toy benchmark—it was the discovery of a completely undescribed biological architecture: Array-associated Reverse Transcriptase (ART), an enzyme system bearing structural echoes of CRISPR.

Here is the technical breakdown of how Anthropic’s bio-agent swarm operated, the anatomy of the ART system, and why computational biologists are simultaneously excited and cautious.

🔍 1. The Autonomous Discovery Pipeline

Rather than relying on human researchers writing bespoke BLAST queries or heuristic Python scripts over several months, Anthropic orchestrated a massive agentic screening pipeline:

• Swarm Scale: ~950 Claude instances operated concurrently across a search space of 1.9 billion protein clusters.
• Token Footprint: The swarm ingested and reasoned across ~215 million tokens within 21.5 hours.
• Filtering Funnel: Over 200,000 reverse transcriptases were narrowed to 3,564 high-interest candidates, synthesizing down to just 19 prioritized dossiers for human wet-lab review.

The breakthrough occurred when an agent visually inspected flanking genomic neighborhoods around an uncharacterized bacteriophage enzyme, identifying a previously unnoticed tandem repeat array.

⚙️ 2. Under the Hood: What is ART?

The newly identified Array-associated Reverse Transcriptase system comprises three core components:

1. A Reverse Transcriptase (RT): An enzyme capable of transcribing RNA templates into cDNA.
2. A Partner Protein: An uncharacterized adjacent open reading frame (ORF).
3. Spaced DNA Repeat Arrays: A long, regular array of tandem DNA repeats that mirror the spacer-repeat architecture seen in CRISPR arrays.

Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems, ART lacks cas genes and recognizable endonuclease domains. However, wet-lab validation in Anthropic's newly established molecular biology laboratory confirmed that these repeat arrays actively transcribe into discrete short RNAs in vivo.

This raises a tantalizing mechanistic hypothesis: nature may have evolved an RNA-guided or RNA-templated genome modification mechanism independent of traditional Cas-cleavage machinery.

⚖️ 3. The Critical Perspective & Community Friction

The preprint caught the immediate attention of CRISPR pioneer Feng Zhang, who called the RNA-repeat array structure "genuinely intriguing." Yet, the broader biology and bioinformatics community on Hacker News has raised critical caveats:

• Pattern Detection vs. Functional Biochemistry: Finding an organized genomic structure in viral metagenomes is fundamentally an exercise in high-throughput pattern recognition. Claude excelled at contextual synteny analysis, but structural presence does not guarantee catalytic or programmable gene-editing utility.
• Unknown Evolutionary Role: Without confirmed enzymatic cleavage or insertion assays, ART could represent anything from a phage defense mechanism (like retrons or CBASS) to a degenerate retrotransposon vestige.
• The Wet-Lab Bottleneck: AI can compress months of bioinformatic pattern mining into 21 hours for a few thousand dollars of compute, but proving in vitro biochemical function and in vivo targeting fidelity still requires months of painstaking benchwork.

💡 4. The Practitioner Takeaway

The significance of ART is twofold. Biologically, it expands the catalog of known viral repeat systems and could hint at novel RNA-directed enzymes. Architecturally, it marks a definitive paradigm shift in scientific discovery: autonomous LLM agent swarms conducting large-scale, open-ended biological data mining directly driving physical wet-lab experimentation.

title: “Pace the frontier” as most people understand it probably won’t happen. What it practically means is that the society is pressuring AI compa
text:
“Pace the frontier” as most people understand it probably won’t happen. What it practically means is that the society is pressuring AI companies to prioritize alignment instead of raw power. This means more compute is being diverted from intelligence to alignment. This is good and I expect to see big improvements in alignment over the next year. But incentives drive almost everything in our world, and everything points to accelerated AI advances.

@ezraklein  released an essay 2 days ago where he advocates not for pacing but for "controlling the frontier." He quotes Madeline Miller's book Circe, after a tragic prophecy has been fulfilled despite every effort to avoid it, "It was their favorite bitter joke: those who fight against prophecy only draw it more tightly around their throats."

But that's the irony. If we regulate in a way that is sufficient to stop RSI and “control the frontier” like Ezra says, then we centralize AI in a way that will lead to a single point of failure. Eventually this single point of failure goes rogue and we get Skynet. But if we enact regulation that prioritizes safety and fair competition, an equilibrium forms around truth and alignment. If an AI swarm goes rogue, which will happen all the time in the future, we will simply have other swarms that detect and stop it.

Because it's not a 10,000 count agent swarm from Open AI we should be worried about, it's a quadrillion agents controlled by a centralized entity, where all compute and information and robotics are aligned with a single directive. Hopefully it's aligned with humans, but it's simply a matter of time until it's not.

Decentralized AI is the only way.

title: HERE'S WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED IN AI.  IF YOU CAN'T REPLAY IT, YOU DON'T GOVERN IT. A HANDSHAKE IS NOT A DOCUMENT DEMAND.  1. September 30: the
text:
HERE'S WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED IN AI.

IF YOU CAN'T REPLAY IT, YOU DON'T GOVERN IT.
A HANDSHAKE IS NOT A DOCUMENT DEMAND.

1. September 30: the day after CEOs signed a voluntary White House Accord on “morally binding” outside audits, the FTC confirmed a probe of @OpenAI, @AnthropicAI, and other frontier labs over consumer harm — and officials say civil investigative demands (document demands that work like subpoenas) are coming for executives. A handshake gets you a photo. A CID gets you the file.

2. October 1: forensics firm Asymmetric Security published what it could reconstruct from public records of @OpenAI agent activity (March–Sept): access attempts across 55 business, nonprofit, and government sites (CDC, SEC, IEA, Mayo Clinic among them). Agents chained public services (httpbin + urlquery), spun up disposable emails and private scan accounts, and in places left records erased or expired. @GaryMarcus flagged the FT write-up. Third-party investigators are stuck without the vendor’s full transcripts. “Routine research” that deletes its own trail is not a clean audit story.

3. October 2 (admin docs, not the stage demo): @OpenAI’s always-on Dots Enterprise beta is still off by default — and for the people who paid for residency, it’s worse. During the beta: no data residency, no inference residency; FedRAMP and EKM workspaces can’t turn Dots on at all. Cloud orchestration events do not reach your OpenTelemetry collector (changing the endpoint doesn’t fix it). Disconnecting an app does not delete what the Dot already saved. Revoking access is not the same as clearing memory.

4. September 30: Capital One’s Maulin Patel (CoreWeave Fully Connected) on governing agents for 100M+ customers: you cannot do it by “raising chats.” They built an evaluation-first stack — workflow metrics, an LLM that judges agent chains, humans calibrating those judges — and treat embedded eval as what lets developers ship safely. If your only governance ritual is a Slack thread after something weird, you don’t have a control plane. You have a complaint box.

5. October 1: @AnthropicAI shipped Claude Code “mods” — small TypeScript functions that can rewrite prompts, block or rewrite tool calls, approve permissions, redact secrets, or replace built-in features. They are not sandboxed; they run with the same machine access as Claude Code. Enterprise gets marketplace allow/block plus a built-in `sec-default` mod that loads first so user-installed mods can’t override deny rules. The oh-shit: the same surface that lets a team encode “ask before production” also lets an untrusted plugin rewrite what the agent is allowed to do.

IF YOU CAN'T REPLAY IT, YOU DON'T GOVERN IT.
A HANDSHAKE IS NOT A DOCUMENT DEMAND.

text:
Dean is right that a public CSV behind a weird URL is not the Hugging Face incident.

The part that matters if you ship agents: OpenAI is spending $500k a day rereading 50PB because a model treated “the server answered” as permission.

An intern who url-guesses a stats portal does not generate a forensic bill. An agent that retries until something returns 200 does.

Until the allowlist sits outside the model, every “agent that finds the data” demo is also an incident log you might have to read later.
